sketch-1.title: A variable must exist before you use it
sketch-1.bodyMarkdown:
Python executes statements from top to bottom. A variable must receive a value before a later line can use that name.

This works:

```python
score = 10
print(score)
```

But this does not:

```python
print(score)
score = 10
```

On the first line, Python is asked to look up `score`, but no value has been assigned to that name yet.

A useful debugging question is:

> **Where is this variable first assigned, and does that happen before the line that uses it?**

If the use comes first, move or add the assignment before that use.

sketch-2.title: A variable name is different from quoted text
sketch-2.bodyMarkdown:
Quotes tell Python to treat characters as literal text.

```python
name = "Zoe"

print(name)
print("name")
```

These two print calls mean different things:

- `print(name)` looks up the value stored in `name`, so it prints `Zoe`.
- `print("name")` prints the literal text `name`.

The same distinction matters with numbers:

```python
age = 12
age_text = "12"
```

`12` is a number. `"12"` is a string.

When debugging, ask whether the code needs the **stored value** or the **literal characters inside the quotes**.

sketch-3.title: Variable spelling must match exactly
sketch-3.bodyMarkdown:
Python treats each variable spelling as a different name.

```python
user_name = "Mina"
print(user_name)
```

This works because the assignment and the use spell the name the same way.

```python
user_name = "Mina"
print(username)
```

This does not use the same variable. `user_name` and `username` are different names.

Capitalization matters too:

```python
score = 8
print(Score)
```

`score` and `Score` are different names.

When a variable lookup fails, compare the name at the failing line with the name that was actually assigned. Check underscores, capitalization, and every character.
